title: Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins
hook: Banda strikes coins and seals in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh
tomorrow: Land to those who work it

segments.voice: Yesterday, a field outside Sirhind, and an ending that arrived but couldn't give back what was lost. Your line was it came. Who did you remember who's still waiting? Today, something small enough to hold in your palm. Day eight hundred forty-one.

Take a coin out of a pocket or a purse and turn it over. There's usually a name on it, or a face, or a seal: whoever claims the right to say this metal is worth something. A coin says who rules here. So it means something that once Banda Singh held territory, he made his base in the hills at a fort called Lohgarh, and from there he struck coins and stamped seals. The question is whose name went on them. Today: Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins.
screen: `TURN A COIN OVER.` → `A NAME SAYS WHO RULES HERE.` → `COINS STRUCK AT LOHGARH.`

segments.voice: A coin was one way a new power announced itself. Banda Singh now had a fort, an army and lands under his hand, and he could have stamped his own name. He didn't. Sikh tradition says the coins and the seal were struck in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. The first Guru and the tenth. Not Banda Singh. Remember the instructions tradition says came with the five arrows: never set yourself up as a Guru, and remember you serve the Khalsa. The coins look like that instruction made into metal. The power was real, but the name on it belonged to someone else. The words on his seal were in Persian, and as Sikh tradition reads them, they speak of deg and tegh. The deg is the cooking pot, the great kettle of the langar where anyone can eat. The tegh is the sword, raised to protect. Pot and sword, side by side, as the gift of the Gurus. It's a short summary of what the Khalsa was meant to be: feed people, and defend them. Some readers hear in these coins the stamp of Sikh rule. Others hear something quieter. A man with every chance to make his own name large chose to stamp the names of his Gurus instead. On an ordinary day, the pull is the same in small ways: the report with our name at the top, the credit we'd like to keep. The coins of Lohgarh point the other way.
screen: `HE COULD HAVE STAMPED HIS OWN NAME.` ·`BANDA SINGH STAMPED THE GURUS' NAMES.` · `DEG AND TEGH: POT AND SWORD.` · `FEED PEOPLE, AND DEFEND THEM.` · then, large: `IN THEIR NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a coin. If one is nearby, hold it. If not, picture one. Sit, and let the breath settle. Read what's on it, slowly, side by side. Whose name, whose face, whose words? Then ask what name you'd want stamped on the things you make: your work, your kindness, your choices today. Not your own name necessarily. Maybe someone who taught you. Maybe Waheguru. Hold the coin, or the picture of it, through the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
deg tegh, the cooking pot and the sword. The gift of the Gurus, stamped into the seal Banda Singh struck at Lohgarh, in his Gurus' names. Today's word.
Your line: in their names. Today, when you finish something good, name the person who taught you to do it, out loud or in your head. Day eight hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember that Banda Singh Bahadur struck coins and a seal at Lohgarh in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh rather than his own, and the words deg and tegh are still used for the Khalsa's twin duty to feed and to protect.
